meta.title: Landing On It, Not Just Including It
meta.summary: Including the characteristic note in a scale isn't the same as leaning on it in a phrase — where you stop is what makes a mode sound like itself.

spans.text: Play every note of A Dorian over
, up and down, and end every phrase back on
. It'll sound like A minor with a passing
was there the whole time. It was never absent. It was just never arrived at.
This pathway has made that exact argument once already, one level up.
said a note set has no home until something outside it decides — a held root, a chord that won't move.
said the same thing for major against minor, one pathway back. Emphasis decides the tonic. It turns out emphasis decides the colour too, for exactly the same reason.
There are four ways to lean on a note, and each one is something your hand actually does:

items.text: End a phrase on it and let it ring — the strongest of the four by a distance.
Hold it while the second chord is underneath it, instead of passing through on the way to somewhere else.
Begin a phrase on it instead of on the root.
Approach from a step above and a step below and land on it, so the ear hears the target twice before you arrive.

spans.text: Time it with the chord underneath and the whole thing gets easier. Every vamp with a note to lean on puts that note inside its second chord — the
chord's. Landing there while that chord is sounding gets you the mode's colour and the chord's own note in the same instant.
Phrygian is the one place this runs into a wall it built for itself. The
is both Phrygian's characteristic note and one of the two notes that fight its own

— a half step above the root is exactly what makes it the note the mode is named for, and exactly what makes it grind against home. Of the seven, Phrygian is the only one where the note you're meant to lean on is also a note you're meant to move through.

Ionian and Aeolian give you nothing to lean on this way, and that's not a shortfall — it's what being the reference means. What they ask for instead is the other half of the same skill: a note to move through rather than land on, the
in the other, both already covered in
The Note That Fights the Chord

props.caption: Land on the F# every time the D comes round, and on nothing else — let the rest of the loop pass you by.

spans.text: . That grind is Phrygian's whole name in one interval, and it's exactly why the mode needs the
chord underneath it rather than the

Here's the check, and it takes thirty seconds. Play the same seven notes over the same vamp again, and this time never stop on the characteristic note — land everywhere else instead. It comes out sounding like the plain scale it's nearest to, every time. That gap, between including a note and leaning on it, is the difference between playing the notes of a mode and actually sounding like one. Try it against a held root on
before you do anything else with it.
